governing_question: What has to work every single day for an Arkansas household to actually be prosperous?
shared_role: They are systems that convert Arkansas' productive capacity into the conditions households need to live, work, build, own and participate.
landing_definition: A Productive Arkansas is not a state that tries to make everything itself. It is a state that understands what it must be capable of doing, what it can profitably do for the world, what it can safely depend on others to do, and how all of those choices ultimately affect Arkansas' households.
efficiency_resilience: Efficiency determines how well a system performs when conditions are favorable. Resilience determines whether the system still belongs to the people when conditions are not.

productive_systems_test.q: Can households pay without destroying Prosperity Surplus?
Where markets operate, can meaningful competition exist?
Who owns productive assets and receives returns?
What happens if an outside supplier fails?
What does it do to Income · Cost · Security · Ownership · Time?

misconception_box.title: So government runs all the essential systems?
misconception_box.explain: Essentiality answers: How important is the function? It does not answer: Who should own it? Ownership must follow function, market structure, law, risk and evidence.

sections.heading: Before the Rivers family gets to work
prose: Start with an ordinary morning. Before anyone in the Rivers household earns a dollar: water comes from the faucet; electricity powers the house; food is available; someone lives in a home; the road is usable; a vehicle starts—or transportation exists; a phone connects; internet works; children can be cared for; healthcare exists if something goes wrong.
Then one of them goes to work. We usually call the job 'the economy.' But an enormous productive system had to function before the workday even began.
The economy isn't merely where people work. It is the network that makes productive life possible.

sections.heading: The eight systems
prose: Food. Energy. Housing. Healthcare. Transportation. Water. Digital. Care.

Do not describe them as eight government responsibilities. They are eight systems involving different combinations of households, private businesses, nonprofits, local government, state government, federal government, cooperatives, utilities, institutions, and markets.
That distinction matters.

sections.heading: Apply one Productive Systems Test
prose: Rather than eight ideologies, teach one analytical tool.
For every system ask: Access? Affordability? Capacity? Quality? Competition? Ownership? Dependency? Resilience? Public purpose? Household effect on Income · Cost · Security · Ownership · Time?
Not: Public or private?
But: What function are we trying to accomplish, what institutional arrangement accomplishes it best, and what happens to the household?

sections.heading: Food — abundance can coexist with dependency
prose: Arkansas produces enormous agricultural value. Agricultural production isn't identical to a complete food system.
Land → inputs → farm → aggregation → processing → storage → distribution → retail → household.
A state can produce commodities while depending heavily on outside systems for processing, distribution, or finished food.

We investigated food hubs not because 'local food is always better' — Stage 4 killed that — but to ask whether greater Arkansas processing/aggregation capacity could retain more productive capability and improve resilience.
Possibly — but not yet proven as public cash. COUNTABLE = $0. The food-hub investigation remains closed.

sections.heading: Strategic capacity
prose: Sometimes the cheapest normal-day system isn't necessarily the safest crisis-day system. That doesn't justify inefficient self-sufficiency.
What productive capacity is worth maintaining because losing it would make Arkansas dangerously dependent during disruption?
That's Strategic Capacity — not autarky. Arkansas shouldn't manufacture everything it consumes. Trade is enormously valuable.
The objective is to understand which dependencies are harmless and which become single points of failure.

sections.heading: Energy — production isn't the same as resilience
prose: Arkansas can produce energy and still have vulnerable households or infrastructure.
Distinguish: energy production, affordability, reliability, resilience, ownership, and external income.
Energy could become an external-income opportunity. It is not COUNTABLE public revenue today.

sections.heading: Housing — prosperity multiplier or prosperity absorber
prose: Connect to Chapter 2. Suppose Arkansas succeeds — wages rise, people move in, jobs grow — but housing supply doesn't.
More money competes for limited housing; prices and rents rise; Prosperity Surplus gets absorbed.
Housing capacity must grow with prosperity or housing can consume the prosperity we create.
Land, infrastructure, zoning/rules, finance, materials, labor, construction, insurance, ownership/rental, maintenance — housing is a production system, not merely 'build more houses.'

sections.heading: Land — the thing we cannot manufacture
prose: Buildings can multiply. Land cannot. Location creates value. Roads, schools, businesses, and population can increase surrounding land values.
This creates difficult questions about ownership, development, speculation, taxation, infrastructure, and public-created value.
Do not solve Georgism or land taxation here. Teach why land behaves differently from ordinary manufactured goods. Deeper questions live in the Explorer and Unabridged.

sections.heading: Healthcare — access without capacity isn't access
prose: Stage 4 finding: Access without capacity can produce queues instead of care.

Imagine government gives everyone the ability to pay for an appointment — but there are no additional physicians, nurses, clinics, or hospital capacity. Financial access increased. Physical access did not.
Healthcare requires people, facilities, equipment, geography, finance, insurance/payment, transportation, preventive capability, emergency capability. System, not slogan.

sections.heading: Rural healthcare exposes fixed-cost economics
prose: A hospital has substantial fixed costs — facilities, equipment, staff, emergency capability, regulatory systems — whether every bed is full or not.
A thinly populated region can need healthcare capacity that pure volume economics struggles to support.
This doesn't automatically prove government ownership. It demonstrates why essential service + thin market can create a structural financing problem.
Apply the ownership decision tree rather than prescribing a model.

sections.heading: Transportation — distance is a household cost
prose: A household may have inexpensive housing but spend enormous money, time, fuel, vehicle depreciation, and opportunity cost getting to work, school, healthcare, food, childcare.
The cost of a place includes the cost of reaching the rest of your life.
Transportation is part of household prosperity.

sections.heading: Transportation is also market infrastructure
prose: Roads, rail, waterways, airports, and freight systems connect Arkansas production to markets.
Transportation has two simultaneous roles: household mobility and productive market access — linking physical infrastructure directly to external income.

sections.heading: Water — invisible until it fails
prose: Water systems support households, agriculture, industry, healthcare, fire protection, development. Much of the infrastructure is invisible. So are maintenance liabilities.
A community can appear financially healthy while underground systems deteriorate.
That's why Constitutional Capitalism uses an Intergenerational Balance Sheet. Deferred maintenance can make today's budget look cheaper by sending the bill to tomorrow.

sections.heading: Digital infrastructure — modern economic geography
prose: Broadband can connect people to education, work, healthcare, markets, government, finance, information.
Connectivity alone isn't capability. A fiber line doesn't guarantee digital skills, affordable service, useful applications, cybersecurity, or economic opportunity.
Infrastructure + human capability + markets.

sections.heading: Digital dependency
prose: A community increasingly dependent on digital systems becomes vulnerable to outages, cyberattack, vendor failure, data loss, and monopoly/platform dependence.
Don't open a cybersecurity policy book. Teach the principle: The more essential a system becomes, the more seriously we must understand its failure modes.
That's the Dependency Matrix in plain English.

sections.heading: Care — the infrastructure hiding inside the household
prose: Childcare, elder care, disability support, family caregiving are often treated as private family matters outside 'the economy.'

If a parent cannot work because childcare is unavailable, care capacity affects labor supply. If someone leaves employment to care for an aging parent, care affects household income. If a worker spends hours coordinating services, care affects time.
Care is both human work and economic infrastructure.
Don't turn that into 'government must provide all care.' An economic model ignoring care is measuring an incomplete economy.

sections.heading: The Dependency Matrix
prose: Rows: Food, Energy, Housing, Healthcare, Transportation, Water, Digital, Care.
Columns: Local capacity, Regional capacity, National dependence, Single-point exposure, Replacement time, Household consequence, Essential-function status.
Use KNOWN / PARTIAL / UNKNOWN where necessary. Do not fabricate completeness.
We cannot manage dependencies we refuse to see.

sections.heading: Production Balance Sheet
prose: For each productive system: What does Arkansas possess? What does Arkansas lack? What is deteriorating? What is growing? What depends heavily on outsiders?
We have the architecture — not a magically complete statewide ledger.

sections.heading: Ownership by function
prose: Does Constitutional Capitalism want government to own these systems? No. Make this unmistakable.

Essential does not mean publicly owned. Food is essential — that doesn't mean state grocery stores. Housing is essential — that doesn't mean government owns everyone's house. Healthcare is essential — that fact alone doesn't determine ownership.
Apply the eight-gate public-investment standard from Chapter 3 where relevant.

Can competitive private markets perform the function well? If yes, strong presumption toward markets. If not, why not — natural monopoly, thin market, strategic capacity, public good, externality, market power? Then determine the narrowest institutional response.

sections.heading: Public utility logic
prose: Imagine five competing companies each digging separate water pipes to every rural house. That can be absurdly inefficient.
Some infrastructure has natural-monopoly characteristics. That can justify regulated private utility, cooperative, municipal utility, authority, or another bounded structure.
The principle isn't ideology. It's matching institution to economic function.

sections.heading: External income versus household essentials
prose: Some systems primarily provide essentials to Arkansans. Others can also sell outside Arkansas — energy, agriculture, manufacturing, technology, tourism, services, research/IP.
Don't sacrifice household affordability merely to maximize exports.
Serve household prosperity while building productive capacity capable of earning income from the wider world.

sections.heading: The Productive Arkansas Flywheel
prose: Capable people → productive systems → goods/services → local + external income → household/business surplus → savings/investment → ownership/capital → stronger productive systems → greater household capability.

Place government around the flywheel, not at its center: sets rules, protects rights, provides legitimate public goods, maintains infrastructure, prevents capture, measures, and fills narrowly demonstrated institutional gaps.

sections.heading: What happens when one system fails?
prose: A major energy outage affects water pumping, food refrigeration, healthcare, digital communications, business, households.
Transportation failure affects food, healthcare, employment, supply chains. Care failure affects labor, household income, time. Water failure affects almost everything.
That's why these are a system of systems.

sections.heading: Efficiency versus resilience
prose: Efficiency determines how well a system performs when conditions are favorable. Resilience determines whether the system still belongs to the people when conditions are not.
Redundancy costs money. Reserve capacity costs money. Local capability can sometimes cost more. Not every redundancy is resilience — some is simply waste.
Classify: essential redundancy, justified insurance, option value, excess capacity, waste.

sections.heading: The weakest-county test
prose: Does this still work somewhere with declining population, limited tax base, aging infrastructure, and thin markets?
Not every service has to physically exist in every county. But every Arkansan needs a viable pathway to essential functions.
Regional systems may sometimes outperform county-by-county duplication. Graceful Contraction: a place doesn't have to grow forever to remain worth living in.

sections.heading: The fastest-growing-county test
prose: Jobs arrive. Population grows. Housing doesn't. Roads clog. Schools fill. Water capacity strains. Healthcare demand rises. Land prices increase.
Growth can destroy some of the prosperity that created it.
Growth Absorption Capacity: a prosperous state must be able to absorb success.

sections.heading: One Arkansas, different places
prose: Avoid promising identical physical systems everywhere. The Delta, Northwest Arkansas, Central Arkansas, the Ozarks, the River Valley, South Arkansas — different geography, industry, density, resources, and population trajectories.

Constitutional Capitalism doesn't require sameness. It requires the same questions: Does the system expand household prosperity? Build capability? Is it resilient? Lawful? Who owns? Who pays? Who benefits? Who bears risk?

sections.heading: Return to the Rivers family
prose: End back at breakfast. The faucet worked. The lights came on. Food was available. The road connected them. The phone worked. Care was possible. Healthcare existed. Housing sheltered them.
None of that felt like 'economic policy.' That's precisely the point.
Prosperity becomes real through systems so dependable that most days we barely notice them.

A Productive Arkansas is not a state that tries to make everything itself. It is a state that understands what it must be capable of doing, what it can profitably do for the world, what it can safely depend on others to do, and how all of those choices ultimately affect Arkansas' households.
Next: government powerful enough to protect this system, capable enough to operate it, constrained enough that neither government nor concentrated private wealth can take it away from the people.
